result.summary: After killing Pelias, Medea burns Creon's palace at Corinth and kills her sons by Jason, then flees on a dragon-drawn chariot. Her flight over Greece and the islands recalls many places tied to metamorphosis myths, ending at Athens.

scenes.title: Medea's crimes and escape
scenes.summary: Medea finds Jason remarried, burns the palace, kills her children and takes off on winged dragons.
scenes.stakes: Medea would face punishment for her murders if she did not escape.

scenes.title: Flight over Greece and islands
scenes.summary: Medea passes places linked to transformation tales: Cerambus, Cea, Hyrie's lake, Pleuron, Calaurea and others.

scenes.title: Ephyre and arrival at Athens
scenes.summary: Medea reaches Ephyre, recalling her revenge, then flies on to Athens.
scenes.stakes: She flees Jason and the consequences of her revenge.

alias_notes.explanation: Rhodes is called Phœbean as sacred to Phœbus Apollo.

notable_quotes.reason: The boy's bitter curse before leaping and becoming a swan.

analysis.text: Medea's vengeance climaxes in infanticide, yet she escapes, while her route catalogues metamorphosis myths.
The catalogue of places shows Ovid's learned use of Hellenistic mythographic and aetiological traditions.

legacy.text: Medea's killing of her children inspired Euripides' earlier tragedy and Seneca's Medea, which Ovid's version echoes.

fun_facts.text: Ovid is thought to have written a lost tragedy Medea, praised by ancient critics.

language_notes.text: The son of Phillyra is the centaur Chiron, tutor of heroes, who lived on Mount Pelion.
The flood of Deucalion is the Greek great flood, survived by Deucalion and Pyrrha; Cerambus was said to escape it by being turned into a winged beetle.
Bacchus (the Greek Dionysus) is said to have hidden a stolen bullock by disguising it as a stag on Ida.
The Coan women grew horns after Hercules' cattle passed; the Telchines were Rhodian sorcerers whose gaze blighted things, and Jupiter drowned them by sending them beneath his brother Neptune's sea.
The boy is Cycnus. Phyllius performed tasks for him as a lover, then refused the last gift, the bull.
"Thou shalt wish that thou hadst given it" is a threat: Cycnus leaps and becomes a swan, leaving Phyllius to regret.
"Was {one day} to lie" looks ahead: Menephron's incest is a future event, told as a transformation tale.
Pirenian refers to Pirene, the famous spring of Corinth; Ephyre is an old name for Corinth.
The city of Pallas is Athens, sacred to Pallas Minerva. Titanian dragons suggest descent from the Sun, a Titan and Medea's grandfather.

context_notes.text: Medea, a Colchian sorceress, helped Jason win the Golden Fleece. Corinth is where he abandoned her to marry Creon's daughter.
Killing her own children is Medea's most notorious act, and the poem reports it briefly and without comment.
Calaurea was an island sacred to Latona, mother of Apollo and Diana; its king and queen became birds.
The persons named here are all said to have been turned into birds; Athens is where Medea next takes refuge with King Aegeus.

literary_notes.text: Listing places by their transformation myths makes her flight a tour of metamorphosis, a favorite Ovidian device.
"Was destined to wonder" anticipates the daughter's change into a dove before it is told.
A tale of people growing from mushrooms sits oddly beside Medea's arrival at the place of her crimes, which it does not mention.
"Wicked sword" and "barbarously" give the narrator's judgement of Medea, stressing her cruelty.
The narrator addresses Phineus and Periphas directly, an emotional gesture before the next transformation story.
